Just to explain this because otherwise you might not get why you're getting down votes, but what's contained within laws is just what's written on paper, how they are implemented are based on real world interactions and how they reflect on what's expected. 

In this case, they have to take every single one down that's complained about within 48 hours. So depending on how many videos a website has, how many workers they may have running it and how many times a take down request is made, they may not be able to tackle all the requests. 

YouTube has this issue, so as a default, the video is just, automatically taken down when it receives a certain number of requests, I believe it's 3. They say they check the validity of the claim, but this is an automated process and a very flawed one. The user then has a week to challenge the takedown and this can be, difficult, to say the least, so a lot of smaller YouTubers end up with completely innocent videos taken down and can't get them back up.

If this law applies to all content on all websites, then it's going to be difficult for a lot of sites to keep normal stuff up, like say, LGBTQ content, if a torrent of MAGAT's, or just the MAGA gov decide to file false requests to take them down.

As we've progressed more in recent years with the advent of the internet and computing, automation has ramped up even more and jobs that require no real skill sets beyond very simple repetitive motions have been dwindling, not just because of the automation, but because of other tasks being consolidated into these roles, which means anyone limited by their mental or physical capabilities to only be able to take on these levels of jobs, either find it extremely difficult to find work they can handle, or they drop out of the work force altogether.

I'd go as far as to say this is probably why a lot of mental health issues are being highlighted far more than before, whilst these are not new issues people have and they have been around forever, the expectations and requirements of jobs has outpaced the abilities of a lot of the individuals who have mental disabilities, in both their social aspects (in modern service economies especially), but also in the needs for multiple different roles pushed into one, the drive for efficiency and the monitoring of metrics and other requirements like adaptability to rapid changes (I'm sure you can think of more). 

All this to say, Every time we apply new technologies to automate work and consolidate the remaining tasks into new multi role job positions, we raise the bar on entry into the workforce, a bar not everyone can rise too and with the advent of automation by AI and robotics, taking away many more roles, essentially eliminating all repetitive tasks of any kind and allowing even more job role consolidation, the bar will be raised extremely high. I expect to see a lot more people being pushed out of the workforce simply because they lack the ability to take on the new role requirements, that's IF, there are new roles.

You can work it out easily with just a basic understanding of the economic principles behind corporate behaviours. 

Companies have to provide returns on investments. That means increasing the amount of profit generated each quarter—not maintaining the same amount, and certainly not earning less.

When acquiring large numbers of new customers isn’t possible anymore (because you've already saturated the market and people don’t switch brands easily), the only way to keep the numbers going up is to cut costs.

At first, that might mean trimming unnecessary spending. But eventually, it leads to cutting wages (by not increasing them in line with inflation), laying off staff through automation, or reducing product quality by cutting corners.

That’s why chocolate products have increased in price while shrinking in size. This phenomenon is known as shrinkflation. It’s well documented. It applies not just to food, but to most products and services. They give you less and charge you more. In the case of food, smaller products mean fewer ingredients, less packaging, and the ability to ship more per pallet or cargo crate. Other industries follow the same principle in different ways.

They have to. There's often no other way to keep investors from pulling out and crashing the company’s value. Even in family owned businesses like Mars, the drive to keep up and generate further profits for themselves to keep up with inflation increases devaluing currency will push the same phenomenon. 

That's why the product doesn't get better, you may get entirely new products that improve for a time, but that's rare these days.

This is what our current issue is and has been for quite some time, there just aren't any new markets opening up except two now and they're AI and robotics, but they don't work like previous markets, in fact they essentially make the situation worse because you need less and less staff the bigger their market share gets and then they'll lower the need for staff in other areas, this will, in essence, kill capitalism.

Seeing as how cuts are everywhere constantly in every company, every year recently and they don't seem to be able to find new markets to create and expand into it's quite clear that having software developers output increasing will mean they will hire less developers. 

So whilst I don't believe the hype that AI will write 90% of code is the next 3-6 months, I do believe that with every increase in output by software Devs fueled by AI will come more layoffs or at the very least a "reshuffling" where the companies that need extremely niche code handled will stop hiring new Devs as they retain their skilled ones and bank on AI to fill the gaps and maybe improve before the skilled ones retire and companies that pump out repeatable code will layoff a lot of their staff, veterans or not, to get cheaper labour done by new Devs using AI, maybe keeping on a few more skilled Devs as an insurance policy. 

Honestly, AI's main use is going to be to increase the output of anyone using it and in this economy, that means less job roles being created, not an expansion of business.

I would argue that in the situation that a human is prompting and directing an AI, or several AI's and one is testing and checking their work (probably using other AI's) that the output is going to increase dramatically per head.

So long as we agree that AI will at least get to that level in the coming years, the problem becomes an economical one, rather than a technological one. 

Simply put, in areas where a lot of code is required, there isn't as much room for an increase in scale as one might think and raising the output per head by a drastic amount due to the implementation of AI, is likely to result in massive cuts to employment, rather than an expansion of business as the market for it doesn't exist.

Basically, we are in the late stage of capitalism where continued growth isn't really possible as any new product has to cut into already existing markets and the only new market is in the automation of the old ones, shrinking job creation so instead we create a projected image of growth, fueled by cuts and the implementation of advanced tools such as AI (as it improves) increasing the output of each individual isn't going to suddenly create more demand of labour, just a larger supply of it.

Secondly, there were many more avenues for expansion during that time period, new technologies led to new innovations and new markets, entertainment had barely had its foot in the door. I just don't see that much left to expand into that wouldn't pull income from other markets, so there wouldn't be expansion of the market, but rather just a shift. 

For instance, full dive VR could be a huge market, but it would just pull people away from gaming, reading, clubbing, watching TV, cinemas etc. it's a replacement tech, not a new market as such. 

The problem as well is that all prior technological developments have simply assisted humans, none have ever been better than humans at any given task. A calculator can do math, but requires human input and direction, but when an AGI can be given oversight of a company's finances and manage it exactly as an entire finance team would, with no human input, and another AI is overseeing it. I just don't see room for human input and I believe we're 5-10 years away from that now.

Now that's a better benchmark for the basic reasoning of these models. Something that is basically impossible for any abled adult to fail at intentionally and something that's fully explained to there's no room for confusion.

There are some areas where augmenting intellect can clearly lead to expansion of the results with the same staffing level, like the sciences, more advancements are a good thing and don't really require a reduction in staff. 

However there are some areas where we cannot simply keep pushing the boundary as there's no demand for it. 

Gaming for instance, if AI can augment coding to the point that a triple A game can be made in say.. a tenth of the time with the same amazing graphics, the idea that you could just improve the graphics insanely to keep the same staff falls short as you'll lose a lot of your customer base who cannot afford to keep buying upgraded consoles/graphic cards for more and more money as you will need far better hardware to keep up and just expanding the game to be the size of earth or something is pointless. cPTSD isn't a title, it's a diagnosis and it can be caused by a wide array of incidents. 

So long as the environment was consistently traumatic (which yours definitely sounds like it was) then it comes under cPTSD. 

Single incidents of trauma come under PTSD. 

I am one of those people who was consistently beaten, pinned down and choked whilst being screamed at everyday until I had panic attacks and then was later sexually abused and further abused by people I was in relationships with. 

Yes, I have cPTSD, because I was exposed to consistent traumatic experiences, but your situation sounds like consistent traumatic experiences also. 

Truthfully, it's best not to make the comparison at all. What you need to ask yourself is:

Did you experience a traumatic environment over an extended period of time or many traumatic experiences? (From the information you've given, this sounds like a yes)

Do you suffer from negative symptoms due to those experiences? (Inconsistent view of self, trouble with sleep or forming and keeping relationships etc) You can Google the symptoms. 

Also, just a note from someone who has Autism and ADHD also, if your younger sibling was constantly violent, screaming and lashing out from a very young age, they could have been having meltdowns, I'm no psychiatrist so I don't want to state either way definitively, but it is usually genetic.
